citation: Eakin H, Methner N, Shearing C (2026). Urban affluence and the evolving social contract: insights from adaptation to drought in South Africa. Regional Environmental Change. doi:10.1007/s10113-026-02608-9
Yeni S (2023). The community behind the gates: social cohesion and ubuntu in residential gated communities in Greenstone Hill, Johannesburg. PhD thesis, University of Johannesburg

claims.text: Where rates and taxes are read as misappropriated, high payment generates an entitlement that the municipality owes rapid preferential service, so loud mobilisation is met with faster response and any new collective policy is read as something the state must manage on the payer's behalf and protect them from.
evaluative_rules: Judge a service by whether the rates paid buy rapid, preferential treatment
objections: Why should I carry the cost of a policy that the City should be running for me?

readings.text: If a new collective policy is introduced, someone who pays high rates and sees that money as misappropriated would read it as something the state must manage on their behalf and protect them from, because they already feel the government should protect them.

Someone who believes their high rates deserve really great service would weigh a new collective policy by whether it brings rapid preferential service to their area, since they see faster response as tied to their payment.

If a new collective policy requires residents to take over responsibility, someone who already feels the government has put a lot of responsibility on them would be less open to it, because they see pushing the city as their burden.

Someone who accepts that even a completely efficient city would take a long time to reach an equitable state would weigh a new collective policy conditionally, open to it only if it acknowledges that those who have enjoyed privileges the most have got to pay for it.

claims.text: Self-supply through boreholes and tanks insulates a household from restrictions, so it stops treating collective restrictions as binding on itself, disengages from the shared saving effort, and reads any new collective policy as not its problem while pursuing off-grid autonomy instead.
evaluative_rules: Judge a collective restriction by whether you are self-supplied and therefore outside it
objections: Is it really my problem when I am not drawing on the system?

readings.text: Someone who says they did not have to abide by harsh restrictions because of their borehole would weigh a new collective water policy as not their problem and likely ignore it.
If a person values sovereignty and getting off the grid to save themselves from dealing with Council, they would read a new collective policy as another Council matter to avoid rather than join.
Someone who shrugs and asks whether it is really their problem would be less open to a new collective policy unless it directly threatened their own supply.

If a person recognizes that more autonomous households leave Council carrying infrastructure costs, they might weigh a new collective policy as something that could raise costs for those who are not autonomous.

claims.text: Shared scarcity and fear of running dry make following the rules a matter of everyone's benefit, so residents conserve and answer coordinated municipal messaging as one team, and read a new policy as a partnership between residents and government rather than a service delivered to them.
evaluative_rules: Judge a policy by whether it treats residents and government as partners sharing one scarce resource
objections: Does this ask everyone to play their part, or does it let some opt out?

readings.text: Someone who stood in the same queue and got the same liters as everyone else would read a new policy by asking whether it keeps that same-queue fairness, and would weigh it more openly if it does not let money or status change what each household gets.

If the fear of carrying twenty-five liters and the stress of buckets, basins and dead plants is still present, a new policy would be weighed by whether it reduces that carrying and anxiety, and would be read more cautiously if it leaves households to manage that strain alone.

Someone who learned that rules had to be followed for everyone's benefit and not only yours would read a new policy as a shared set of rules, and would weigh it by whether it asks every household to play the same part rather than leaving some to do more.

If the real recipe for success is collective action and partnership between residents and government, a new policy would be weighed by whether it builds that resident-government partnership, and would be read less openly if it is framed only as government delivering to residents.

claims.text: Where crime is read as rampant and the state as unable to control it, safety is treated as something only gates and enforced estate rules can deliver, so households trade space and money for security and order, and read any new policy or product by whether it preserves that safety, order and property standard.
evaluative_rules: Judge a product or policy by whether it preserves safety, order and property standards
objections: Does this keep the space safe and orderly, or does it let the outside in?

readings.text: Someone who sees estate rules as the mechanism that keeps the community safe and orderly would weigh any new policy or product by whether it reinforces those rules and the standard of care they enforce.
If safety is understood as something only gates and enforced estate rules can deliver, a new policy or product would be read first for whether it preserves that safety, order and property standard.
Someone who treats the estate as a trade of space and money for security would be less open to a new policy or product that asks them to give up more space, money or the order they paid for.
If the state is read as unable to control crime, a new policy or product that depends on state delivery or on conditions outside the gate would be weighed as unreliable.

region: Cape Town (southern suburbs) and Greenstone Hill, Johannesburg, South Africa
confidence: Two small qualitative South African studies: 11 homeowner interviews in affluent Cape Town suburbs (drought water) and residents of two Johannesburg gated estates (security). For water and security the reasoning was heard; for power and solar it is an untested extension of the same reasoning, not a finding. Magnitudes unknown.
subject: comfortable city homeowners paying to supply for themselves what the municipality or state fails to deliver: water tanks and boreholes, private security and estates, and by extension backup power
borrowed_from: Cape Town homeowners on private water during the drought, and Johannesburg estate residents on paying for gates and guards. The same reasoning (pay to go private because the state fails) is carried over to backup power and solar, which no South African interview study covers for comfortable homes.
year_note: Cape Town drought interviews look back on 2017-2018; the Johannesburg estate fieldwork ran up to 2023.
